ground_truth_witness:
Graph: the icosahedron, verified inside the script to be 12 vertices, 30 edges, 5-regular, connected, with every vertex link a 5-cycle and exactly 20 triangular faces, so V-E+F = 12-30+20 = 2 (a sphere triangulation, hence planar — a legitimate map). Adjacency used: 0:{1,2,3,4,5}, 1:{0,2,5,6,7}, 2:{0,1,3,7,8}, 3:{0,2,4,8,9}, 4:{0,3,5,9,10}, 5:{0,1,4,6,10}, 6:{1,5,7,10,11}, 7:{1,2,6,8,11}, 8:{2,3,7,9,11}, 9:{3,4,8,10,11}, 10:{4,5,6,9,11}, 11:{6,7,8,9,10}.

A legal execution of the Optimal-Color algorithm with 5 colours (every tie-break is permitted by the rule and every colour used is non-conflicting at the moment it is chosen):
 1. select vertex 11 (all ColoredDegrees are 0, all degrees are 5, so the tie is arbitrary) and colour it 1
 2-6. colour its uncoloured neighbours: 10←2, 9←3, 8←4, 7←5, 6←4  (each non-conflicting when chosen)
 7. remove 11
 8. select vertex 5 (ColoredDegree 2, tied, arbitrary) and colour it 5
 9-11. colour its uncoloured neighbours: 4←4, 1←3, 0←2
 12. remove 5
 13. select vertex 3 (ColoredDegree 4, tied with vertex 2 which also has ColoredDegree 4; degrees are equal at 5, so the tie is arbitrary) and colour it 1
 14. STUCK: step (3) must now colour the uncoloured neighbour 2 of vertex 3.

State at failure: v0=2, v1=3, v2=uncoloured, v3=1, v4=4, v5=5, v6=4, v7=5, v8=4, v9=3, v10=2, v11=1.
Recomputed quantities: vertex 2 has degree 5 with neighbours [0,1,3,7,8] carrying colours [2,3,1,5,4]; distinct colours on them = {1,2,3,4,5}, size 5; palette size 5; the set of non-conflicting colours at vertex 2 is EMPTY. The claim says the count of available non-conflicting colours is always >= 1; here it is 0 < 1. The execution is re-verified end to end by an independent replay checker in the script (it re-derives the selection-rule candidate set at every selection, re-checks every colour for conflicts, and asserts the final vertex has zero available colours).
ground_truth_flaw: The proof claims that Player A running the stated Optimal-Color algorithm (pick uncolored vertex of highest ColoredDegree, ties by degree, remaining ties arbitrary; color it; then color all uncolored neighbors; remove it) always wins with 5 colors, because "with 5 colors, there will always be a non-conflicting color available to choose, regardless of which non-conflicting sequence of colors have been chosen prior" and because "it does not matter which color from the non-conflicting colors is chosen in each step". A single legal execution of that algorithm on the icosahedron (a planar graph, i.e. a legitimate map) reaches an uncolored vertex whose 5 neighbors carry all 5 distinct colors, so no non-conflicting color exists and Player B wins.
